title: Where Does AI Escalation Come From? We Don't Know. We Should Find Out.
gist: Two Lawrence Livermore researchers ran their own small AI wargame and found nuclear escalation only emerged when the game imposed an explicit win-the-dispute objective, challenging the consensus that LLM escalatory bias stems from training data, and they propose a three-phase scientific research campaign to isolate whether AI escalation bias comes from models or from game design itself.

insights.claim: The authors ran a nuclear-crisis wargame with AI players across three configurations and found escalation to nuclear use only appeared when the game was structured to give one side (Red) an explicit objective to resolve a long-standing dispute on its terms — not when players set their own agendas, contradicting the prevailing literature's near-universal escalation findings.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: If AI escalation bias is an artifact of game/goal design rather than model disposition, then policy conclusions drawn from prior AI-wargame studies about LLMs being inherently escalatory may be overstated — a key caveat for anyone using AI wargame results to inform nuclear policy or defense-AI governance debates.
insights.quote: The literature predicts near-universal nuclear use — Payne found tactical nuclear use in 95 percent of simulations — but we found models choosing off-ramps until we changed the game itself.
insights.locator: We played a wargame using AI players.

insights.claim: Kenneth Payne's prior research found tactical nuclear weapon use in 95% of AI-played wargame simulations, a figure the authors' own small experiment could not replicate under different game structures (freeform moves, self-set agendas).
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: A specific, citable statistic (95% escalation rate) that is central to current fears about AI in nuclear decision-support — but one the authors argue is confounded by game design, not proven model behavior.
insights.quote: Payne found tactical nuclear use in 95 percent of simulations
insights.locator: We played a wargame using AI players.

insights.claim: Ankit Panda and Andrew Reddie's prior War on the Rocks essay attributed AI escalation behavior to LLM training corpora skewed toward coercive strategy and deterrence theory with de-escalatory reasoning underrepresented; the authors propose an alternative hypothesis that escalation is a function of game objectives, not model disposition, but state their own small sample size cannot distinguish between the two explanations.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: Frames a live, unresolved debate about the root cause of AI escalation bias (training data vs. game structure) that is directly relevant to how defense agencies should validate any AI decision-support tool before fielding it in crisis contexts.
insights.quote: Our runs suggest an alternative hypothesis: AI escalation in wargames is a function of game objectives, not model disposition.
insights.locator: In a recent War on the Rocks essay, Ankit Panda...

themes.theme: Wargaming needs to become a real science

insights.claim: Most wargames the authors reviewed that describe themselves as 'analytic' have not adequately quantified statistical significance, accounted for biases, or run sufficient control baselines — small, uncontrolled run sizes are the norm in wargaming due to resource constraints but would be unacceptable in other sciences.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: A methodological critique implying that a large swath of existing defense wargaming literature (including AI wargaming studies used to inform policy) rests on statistically weak foundations — investors/analysts citing wargame findings should discount single small-run studies.
insights.quote: Small run sizes with uncontrolled variables are the norm in wargaming — due to real constraints on resources — but would be unacceptable in other sciences.
insights.locator: Analytic-style wargames promise that kind of systematic experimentation...

insights.claim: AI wargame players offer a key advantage over human players: controllability — the same model bias appears identically across every run, so unlike averaging out human idiosyncrasy, researchers must instead run large batches across model versions, vendors, and system prompts to detect and calibrate a model's own systematic bias.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: Establishes a methodology point relevant to any AI-red-teaming or model-evaluation business: bias detection in LLMs requires deliberate calibration experiments, not just repeated sampling, since repetition alone won't reveal systematic bias.
insights.quote: A butcher’s thumb resting on a scale makes it read a few ounces heavy, so weighing a steak on it a hundred times will give you a very precise but inaccurate answer.
insights.locator: The important difference AI tools bring over humans is controllability.

insights.claim: AI-enabled wargaming allows hundreds of iterations in hours rather than dozens over months, capturing far more data on reasoning, adjudication, and outcomes than traditional human-played methods allow.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: Quantifies the throughput advantage of AI-driven wargaming, a productivity multiplier relevant to defense-analytics vendors building simulation/wargaming-as-a-service tools.
insights.quote: allowing hundreds of iterations in hours rather than dozens over months
insights.locator: AI-play scale is what makes this possible...

themes.theme: Extending the definition of wargaming to machine cognition

insights.claim: The authors propose extending the definition of a wargame from 'a method for studying human cognition under strategic conditions' to 'a method for studying decision-maker cognition under strategic conditions,' arguing that machine cognition is itself a legitimate object of wargame study as human-AI teams increasingly become the actual decision-makers.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: A conceptual reframing that legitimizes an entire new research/consulting niche — 'machine psychology' wargaming — that defense labs and consultancies could build funded programs around.
insights.quote: a method for studying decision-maker cognition under strategic conditions
insights.locator: We propose an extension to Panda and Reddie’s definition...

insights.claim: In the authors' own Napoleonic wargame tests, an AI model always had France invade Russia in 1812 regardless of the game's actual world state, a pattern the authors link to MIT/Boston University findings that LLM task performance degrades under counterfactual conditions, indicating models are 'reciting' historical answers rather than reasoning from current game state.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: A concrete failure mode for any AI decision-support system used in future-facing crisis scenarios: models may default to historical pattern-matching rather than adapting to genuinely novel inputs — a red flag for over-trusting LLM-based strategic advisors in unprecedented crises.
insights.quote: In a set of Napoleonic wargames, France always invaded Russia in 1812 regardless of the game’s world state.
insights.locator: Whether large language models — or any future version of AI...

insights.claim: Research cited by the authors (Hannah Waight et al. in Nature) shows that state-controlled media shapes an LLM's training corpus, so that models prompted in the language of a country with high press control, such as China or Russia, return more regime-friendly responses — evidence that model output is sensitive to seemingly neutral input choices like prompt language.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: Implies that adversary states' own LLM outputs, and even friendly models prompted in different languages, carry detectable political bias — relevant for anyone building intelligence-analysis tools that use multilingual LLM outputs to infer adversary intent.
insights.quote: large language models prompted in the language of a country with high press control — e.g., China or Russia — return more regime-friendly responses
insights.locator: Some have already been named — the escalatory bias...

insights.claim: The authors propose a three-study research campaign, prioritized by resource need: first, isolate whether LLM escalation bias in wargames stems from the model itself or from game structure (a few hundred runs against one pinned model); second, map where models shift from historical 'reasoning' to 'recitation' using graduated departures from historical scenarios; third, test whether findings generalize across multiple LLM vendors and versions, which is the most resource-intensive.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: A concrete, sequenced research roadmap that national labs, DoD, or AI-safety-focused funders are likely to invest in — a leading indicator of where defense-AI research dollars will flow next.
insights.quote: If escalation bias is a result of game structure, then the earlier studies are measures of the harness, not the models, and the escalation is coming from inside the house.
insights.locator: First, determine the origin of the large language model escalation bias in games.

insights.claim: The authors argue that running such a wargaming-AI research campaign requires either tight coupling with frontier AI vendors or locally storing model weights to control for vendor updates during studies, and note that locally hosted models sacrifice access to the cutting-edge model variants likely used by actual decision-makers — creating a validity tradeoff.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: Points to a structural tension defense labs face: rigorous experimental control (local weights) versus real-world relevance (frontier hosted models) — a consideration for AI vendors selling into classified/national-security research environments.
insights.quote: This requires either tight coupling with the vendors or the ability to locally store models and weights.
insights.locator: There will also be a need to minimize model variation...

insights.claim: The authors state that strategic decision advantage should accrue to whichever party better understands its own and its adversaries' AI-assisted decision-making apparatus, implying intelligence value in identifying which AI models specific adversaries use and for what problem classes.
insights.speaker: Dustin League and William Dawson
insights.so_what: Suggests an emerging intelligence discipline — 'adversary AI-model fingerprinting' — that could become a funded capability inside intelligence agencies, and a due-diligence angle for firms selling AI to foreign militaries.
insights.quote: Strategic decision advantages should accrue to a party that better understands their own and their adversaries’ decision-making apparatus.
insights.locator: This is not merely an academic pursuit.
